claims.text: Higher intake of ultra-processed food is associated with a higher risk of overall cardiovascular disease.
Higher intake of ultra-processed food is associated with a higher risk of coronary heart disease.
Higher intake of ultra-processed food is associated with a higher risk of cerebrovascular disease.
Higher intake of unprocessed or minimally processed foods is associated with a lower risk of overall cardiovascular disease.
Ultra-processed beverages are associated with an increased risk of overall cardiovascular disease.
Non-ultra-processed forms of examined food groups show no strong evidence of association with overall cardiovascular disease risk.

evidence.description: Multivariable Cox proportional hazard models showed a hazard ratio of 1.12 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.20; P<0.001) for an absolute increment of 10% in the percentage of ultra-processed foods in the diet across 1409 cases.
Hazard ratio for an absolute increment of 10% in ultra-processed food intake was 1.13 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.24; P=0.02) across 665 cases.
Hazard ratio for an absolute increment of 10% in ultra-processed food intake was 1.11 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.21; P=0.02) across 829 cases.
Multivariable Cox models showed a hazard ratio of 0.91 (95% CI 0.86 to 0.97; P<0.001) for an absolute increment of 10% in unprocessed or minimally processed foods.
Hazard ratio for a 100 g/day increase in ultra-processed beverages was 1.06 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.10; P<0.001) for overall cardiovascular disease.
Analysis of non-ultra-processed counterparts of specific food groups yielded no strong evidence of association with cardiovascular disease risk.

methodologies.name: NutriNet-Santé Cohort Prospective Study Analysis
methodologies.description: A population-based prospective cohort study analyzing dietary intakes from web-based 24-hour records categorized by NOVA classification to evaluate cardiovascular disease risk using multivariable Cox proportional hazard models.
datasets: CépiDC national cause specific mortality registry
conditions: multivariable adjustment for diet quality, lifestyle, and sociodemographic factors

limitations.text: Residual confounding from unmeasured behavioral factors or imprecision in covariate measurement cannot be ruled out due to the observational design.
Causality of the observed associations cannot be established from this observational cohort study.
Misclassification of food items within NOVA categories of ultra-processed food cannot be completely ruled out.
Statistical power was limited for specific sub-types of cardiovascular disease.
The length of follow-up was relatively limited (median 5.2 years), capturing primarily mid-term associations.
Participants in the volunteer cohort were younger, more educated, healthier, and predominantly female compared with the general population, which may lead to selection bias.

future_work.text: Confirm the prospective associations between ultra-processed food intake and cardiovascular disease risk in other large-scale population-based studies and settings.
Investigate the relative impact and cocktail effects of food additives, contact materials, neoformed contaminants, and nutritional composition on cardiovascular disease risk.
Reassess the associations between ultra-processed food intake and risk of cardiovascular disease over longer follow-up durations in the cohort.
